# A synthetic modern draft

The ferry was late again. Marcus stood at the edge of the dock with his hands in his pockets and watched the water, which was flat and gray and didn't seem to be going anywhere. He didn't check his phone. He'd told himself he wouldn't, not until the boat came round the point.

Behind him the café was opening. He could hear the shutters going up, the scrape of a chair, a radio somewhere playing something with too much bass. He didn't turn around. He knew what he'd see: the same three tables, the same chalkboard, the same girl with the nose ring who never remembered his order and never seemed to mind that she didn't.

It was the kind of morning that felt like it was waiting for something.

He thought about the letter. It was in his jacket, folded twice, and he could feel the corner of it against his ribs when he breathed. He hadn't opened it. That was the thing. He'd carried it for three days, through two shifts and a dinner he didn't want to go to, and he still hadn't opened it.

"You're early," someone said.

He turned. It was Dana, holding two coffees, her hair pulled back the way she wore it when she hadn't slept. She held one of the cups out to him and he took it.

"I'm not early," he said. "It's late."

"Same thing, from where I'm standing." She came and stood beside him at the edge of the dock and looked out at the water too. "Did you open it?"

"No."

"Marcus."

"I know."

She didn't say anything else. That was the thing about Dana: she knew when to stop. She drank her coffee and he drank his, and the radio behind them changed to a song he half recognized, and out past the point a gull went up off the water and came back down.

He'd known her for eleven years. He'd known her before the accident and after it, and she was one of the few people who hadn't changed the way they looked at him. She didn't treat him like something that might break. She didn't treat him like anything. She just stood there.

"What if it's nothing?" he said.

"Then it's nothing."

"And if it isn't?"

She shrugged. "Then it isn't. Either way you'll know."

He didn't answer. He looked down at the cup in his hand, at the lid, at the little tab you were supposed to fold back and never did. His thumb found it anyway. He folded it back. It didn't stay.

The ferry came round the point a few minutes later, low in the water, its horn going once, twice. It was a small boat, white once, now mostly the color of rust and old paint. He'd ridden it a hundred times. He'd ridden it the morning his father died and the morning he got the job at the yard and every ordinary morning in between, and it had never once been on time.

"Here we go," Dana said.

They walked down to the end of the dock together. The deckhand threw a line and Marcus caught it without thinking and looped it round the post, the way he'd done since he was a kid. The deckhand nodded at him. He nodded back. Neither of them said anything.

On the boat he found a seat by the rail and Dana sat across from him with her back to the wind. The engine changed pitch and the dock slid away behind them, and the café and the chalkboard and the girl with the nose ring got smaller and then were gone behind the breakwater.

He took the letter out.

It was heavier than it should have been. Good paper, cream-colored, his name typed on the front with no return address. He turned it over. He turned it back.

"You don't have to do it here," Dana said.

"I know."

"I'm just saying."

"I know what you're saying."

He slid his thumb under the flap. The paper tore unevenly and he stopped, and then he kept going, and then it was open and there was a single sheet inside, folded in thirds. He didn't take it out right away. He sat there with the envelope open in his hands and the wind pulling at the edge of the paper, and he waited for something to happen.

Nothing did.

He took the sheet out and unfolded it. It was short, four lines, maybe five. He read it once. He read it again. Then he folded it back up and put it in the envelope and put the envelope back in his jacket, against his ribs, where it had been for three days.

Dana was watching him. She didn't ask.

"It's from my brother," he said.

She waited.

"He wants to meet." He looked out at the water. "He's in the city. He says he's been in the city for a year."

"A year."

"A year." He laughed, but it didn't sound like a laugh. "He's been forty minutes away for a year, and he writes me a letter."

The boat hit a swell and the spray came up over the rail, cold, and he didn't move to wipe it off. Dana reached across and put her hand on his knee, just for a second, and then took it back.

"Are you going to go?"

He didn't know. That was the honest answer, and he almost said it. Instead he said, "I don't know what I'd say to him."

"You don't have to know. You just have to show up."

"That's what people say."

"It's what people say because it's true."

He thought about his brother. Not the brother in the letter, the one who wrote in neat blue ink and said things like *I understand if you need time*, but the other one: the one who'd taught him to tie a bowline on this same ferry, who'd let him steer once when the captain wasn't looking, who'd left one night with a duffel bag and a borrowed car and never called. He thought about that night. He thought about the sound of the car on the gravel, and the way his mother had stood at the window for a long time after, and the way she'd never said his brother's name again, not once, not even at the end.

The island came up out of the haze ahead of them, low and green, the lighthouse a white mark on the point. He watched it get closer. He could see the harbor now, the boats, the line of houses up the hill, the church with the roof they'd been meaning to fix for ten years.

"I'll go," he said.

Dana didn't say anything. She didn't have to. She just nodded, once, and looked out at the island with him, and the ferry's horn went again, twice, the way it always did when it came into the harbor, and the gulls went up off the breakwater all at once and wheeled and came back down.

He kept his hand on his jacket the rest of the way in. He could feel the corner of the envelope against his ribs. It didn't feel heavier. It didn't feel lighter either. It just felt like something he was carrying, and would keep carrying, at least for a while.

When they docked he caught the line again. The deckhand nodded. He nodded back. And then he stepped off the boat and onto the dock and started up the hill toward the house, and he didn't look back, not once, not even when Dana called his name.
